population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. Adults ~268M. Currently on an incretin for any indication: 23.0%, or about 61.6M. Ever used: 30.5%, or about 81.7M. Used and off now: 30.5 − 23.0 = 7.5% of adults, about 20.1M. Age check: 0.20×12 + 0.33×22.5 + 0.24×36 + 0.23×19.5 = 2.4 + 7.43 + 8.64 + 4.49 ≈ 22.95. Income thirds 29/23/17 average to 23.0. Cycling arithmetic: churn continues at the parent's ~40% one-year restart rate, and employer exits added a fresh wave of forced stops, so restarters are now ~38% of current users (0.38×23.0 ≈ 8.7 pp). About 25% of those off now had already cycled once (0.25×7.5 ≈ 1.9 pp). (8.7 + 1.9)/30.5 ≈ 35% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once. Of the ~20M currently off, roughly 7M stopped because of a coverage or price change (job change, employer exclusion, Medicare or Medicaid lockout) rather than a side effect. Payer mix of the 61.6M current users: diabetes/cardiac/OSA/MASH/CKD-coded coverage across all payers ~24.0M; AUD-coded coverage under parity rules (from Aug 2030 approval and earlier off-label EAP routing) ~0.8M; employer obesity coverage ~6.5M; Medicare obesity-only (Continuity Model) ~2.4M; Medicaid obesity ~2.0M; brand cash via TrumpRx/direct ~17.0M; gray market ~8.9M. Sum: 24.0 + 0.8 + 6.5 + 2.4 + 2.0 + 17.0 + 8.9 = 61.6M. Growth came mostly from the cash pill channel and from Medicare age-in, not from new insured coverage. Pediatric: ~0.8% of ~73M under-18s (~0.58M), almost all aged 12+. Growth is slowed by 11 states' minor-prescribing restrictions. Under-12 use is banned outright in 6 of those states and specialist-only elsewhere. Never-users with obesity in the bottom income third remain the largest untreated group: about 38M adults with BMI ≥30 have never used the drug, disproportionately uninsured, rural or hourly workers. About 1 in 3 US children now lives in a household where an adult is on the drug.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the CMS GLP-1 Continuity Model is renewed for 2030–31 at the unchanged $245/month and ~$50 copay, with the same conditions: ≥80% proportion of days covered, ≥5% loss at 6 months, and a 12-month lockout on lapse. Enrolment is ~2.4M obesity-only beneficiaries, up through age-in. Spending: 2.4M × $245 × 12 ≈ $7.1B/yr, now well above CBO's ~$4B/yr baseline, and that gap is a live fight in the 2031 budget. Medicaid: 17 states cover obesity, down from 19 after Missouri and Indiana dropped coverage in 2029 budget cuts, for ~2.0M enrollees. Gross cost: 2.0M × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.9B/yr. The federal share at ~65% FMAP is ≈ $3.8B. Nine states now attach adherence waivers. Semaglutide for AUD (Aug 2030) falls under Medicaid substance-use benefits in all states, and under MHPAEA parity for commercial plans that cover AUD medications.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India has 70+ generic semaglutide brands, injectable and now oral, at ~$8–40/month. Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and most of Southeast Asia sell generics at roughly CAD 60–100 or local equivalents. Chinese generic tirzepatide filings are pending in several emerging markets. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: Prices stalled. TrumpRx and direct prices have been unchanged since 2027–28: injectable semaglutide $199, Zepbound $249–299, oral initial doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) $149, Foundayo maintenance doses $249–299, retatrutide $399. Oral amycretin launched May 2030 at $449/month direct cash (list $1,499), under supply allocation and with waitlists at direct-to-consumer pharmacies. Manufacturers cite oral-peptide API demand (an oral peptide needs many times the API of a weekly injection) and decline further cuts. List prices are unchanged. Employer weight-management coverage fell 44% → 39% (2029) → 36% (2030, Business Group on Health). Most remaining coverage requires a comorbidity code plus a vendor programme. Oral share of new starts has risen from ~35% to ~55%. Gray market: telehealth personal importation of Indian oral and injectable generics at $60–120 is now the largest channel. 503A personalised compounding persists. Research-peptide retatrutide continues at $150–250. Together these serve ~8.9M people (~14% of users), up as cash prices stopped falling. Some prescribers now code AUD to reach parity coverage, and two large PBMs have begun auditing AUD-coded claims that carry no alcohol-history documentation.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, Lilly)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular co-agonist, daily oral (amycretin oral, Novo; approved Apr 2030)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: smoking and nicotine-vaping cessation in adults with overweight or obesity (semaglutide, Sep 2028)
alcohol use disorder in adults regardless of BMI (semaglutide, Aug 2030; ASAM and APA guideline endorsement as a second-line pharmacotherapy, Feb 2030)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: nicotine cessation in normal-weight smokers and vapers
alcohol reduction in heavy drinkers without an AUD diagnosis (off-label since the Aug 2030 label)
microdosing for 'metabolic health' via gray-market telehealth
research-peptide retatrutide in gym and 'recomposition' communities
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care, now banned in 6 states
gambling and compulsive-shopping reduction, case series only and promoted by some telehealth clinicians
drugs.pipeline_note: Oral parity is realised through Novo's oral amycretin. It was filed Feb 2029 after phase 3 and approved Apr 2030, 14 months after filing. Mean loss is ~21% at 72 weeks, matching tirzepatide's ~20–21% and the first pill to do so. It is still short of retatrutide's ~29%. GI tolerability is similar to injectables, and once-daily fasting-state dosing is required. Supply is the constraint, not efficacy. Subcutaneous amycretin was filed alongside and remains under FDA review. Survodutide was filed Mar 2029 and is under review, with a decision expected early 2031; it is not on the market. MariTide (monthly) filed its BLA Jun 2030 and is not eligible for approval before mid-2031. The semaglutide AUD sNDA was filed Oct 2029 on a phase 3 programme that read out mid-2029 (heavy-drinking days reduced ~30% vs placebo, a stronger effect than naltrexone in the subgroup with obesity) and was approved Aug 2030. Lilly's tirzepatide AUD trial is in phase 3. The global incretin market is ~$140B (2030). Growth is volume-driven, with flat US net price and ex-US generic erosion.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Oral amycretin's real-world early GI rates are similar to injectable tirzepatide. Worst with retatrutide top doses and uncontrolled gray-market titration.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic label 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis'.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid loss. Retatrutide real-world incidence is stable at the higher early level.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL ongoing; first bellwether trial set for 2031.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The concern about older adults and women over 60 persists. Bone-density cohort abstracts have not progressed to a formal signal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Retatrutide label recommends resistance exercise and protein counselling; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; no new data changed the picture.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; no US class label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new evidence. Psychiatric monitoring in the AUD trials found no excess.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed from US labels (Jan 2026); not reinstated.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Unquantified. The AUD phase 3 measured craving and drinking, not hedonic tone, so no validated anhedonia scale appears in any pivotal trial. The complaint persists in anti-pharma and body-liberation spaces and in couples-therapy podcasts.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. The AUD label lists routine neuropsychiatric monitoring, as the smoking label does.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Coverage-driven stops remain the commonest cause of discontinuation, swelled by the 2029–30 employer exits. Real-world regain is roughly half of lost weight within a year.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; it underpins the Medicare and Medicaid adherence conditions.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reports continue at retatrutide-level intake reduction. No new pattern with oral amycretin.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; societies recommend baseline and annual labs.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescents; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The cycling question is still unstudied, while ~35% of ever-users have now cycled. The earliest adolescent starters are approaching year five.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; FDA Sentinel cycling study (commissioned 2028) has no readout yet.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cumulative FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~7,000 by mid-2030. The rise tracks gray-market volume, with no new harm type.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion stands; import alerts on Indian API shippers; personal-importation enforcement still mostly unpursued.

safety_ledger.effect: Acquired olfactory and taste dysfunction (hyposmia/dysgeusia) after ≥5 years of continuous GLP-1 RA use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No replication and no refutation. A US claims analysis (2029) could not test it because smell testing is not routinely coded. The Danish–Swedish HR ~1.5 and absolute excess ~2–3 per 1,000 person-years stand.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA PRAC closed its review (Mar 2029) with 'continue monitoring', and the PSUR now tracks it. FDA Sentinel review is ongoing, with no label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Mostly mild and dose-related, as in the trials.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~34% of US households. Snack and confectionery unit volumes are down ~6–7% from 2026 and sugary drinks ~5%. Growth is in protein, fibre, 'small-format' and high-price 'clean' SKUs. Big CPG firms now report 'companion' lines as a segment. Private-label snack makers closed another round of plants in Ohio, Indiana and Kentucky. Discount-grocery basket composition has diverged from premium-grocery baskets more than at any point in Circana's records.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down a further ~4–5% over two years. After the AUD approval, distillers cite 'incretin-driven heavy-drinker attrition' in guidance, and Diageo and Constellation take US brand impairments. Beer is down ~2%. Non-alc keeps growing but does not replace the lost value. Bars in college towns are steady; neighbourhood taverns in the Rust Belt are closing. Tobacco volumes are falling faster than trend, and Altria attributes part of it to cessation prescribing.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat. Half-portion menus are standard. Premium tasting-plate formats thrive in affluent metros, while buffets and value-meal chains lose locations. Fast-casual protein bowls are the growth format. Bar-and-grill chains suffer from lost alcohol attachment.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting, and Torrid closes another ~150 stores. 'Athletic-tailored' cuts (narrow waist, room in shoulders and thighs for muscle) become the premium menswear and workwear silhouette. Mainstream retailers manage high size-churn returns from cyclers. Discount chains keep wide size runs as a core business.

fitness.state: Strength-training studios grow, and premium clubs (Equinox-style) bundle body-composition scans, coaching and telehealth prescribing. Muscle becomes the visible proof that loss was 'done right', which is to say paid for. Budget cardio gyms are flat. Research-peptide sales remain embedded in gym communities.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 36%. Coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiac, OSA, MASH and CKD codes, and, since Aug 2030, AUD under parity. About 1 in 4 large self-funded employers attach BMI or adherence premium differentials ($50–100/month). Pharmacy trend is ~7%. PBMs are building utilisation-management rules for AUD-coded GLP-1 claims.

pharma.state: Lilly is dominant across injectables and Foundayo. Novo regains US momentum with oral amycretin but cannot supply it at scale. Both hold net prices flat and grow on volume. Oral-peptide API capacity is the binding constraint, and Novo is building plants in North Carolina and Denmark. Novo's US sales force shrinks after the end of broadcast DTC advertising for obesity.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Body shape now reads as income. Lean with visible muscle means insured or paid in cash plus a trainer: a professional who 'did it right'. Lean and soft, or 'reta face', means drug without gym, often cash or gray market. Larger bodies are read, often wrongly, as poorer, uninsured or recently dropped. Being off the drug is visible within a year of losing coverage, and coworkers notice.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The tiers are uniforms now. On-drug rates run 29% in the top income third and 17% in the bottom. Coverage-driven cycling concentrates in hourly and contract workers. BMI surcharges fall on warehouse, retail and call-centre workforces at large self-funded employers. In Columbus, Charlotte and Phoenix, recruiters admit off the record that 'executive presence' now includes a gym-lean build. Lawsuits testing weight as a protected class under the Michigan and NYC statutes rise.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Upper-middle-class dinners are small, protein-forward and alcohol-light. Holiday tables split by drug status remain common. In Black church, Mennonite and Southern Baptist communities, the full communal meal has become an explicit marker of belonging and of refusing a class code. Some congregations in Oklahoma and Mississippi run 'full plate Sundays'.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating apps in large metros let users filter by fitness, which is widely read as filtering by class. 'On it / off it' disclosures have spread beyond NY and LA. Couples split by coverage describe mismatched appetite and energy. Low libido is talked about but rarely blamed on the drug.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: With AUD on the label, appetite for food, nicotine and alcohol is officially treatable. The counter-movement has fractured along class lines. Fat liberation in Atlanta and Oakland frames the issue as labour and coverage justice. The 'Made Whole' evangelical movement in Texas and Oklahoma frames it as stewardship of the God-given body. MAHA influencers sell 'natural' alternatives at boutique prices that only the affluent can afford.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: No trial, registry, label or survey measures it. The AUD approval reinforces the frame: reduced wanting is the therapeutic endpoint, and the AUD trials scored craving and drinks, not pleasure. With ~62M current users, any population-level hedonic effect would be large, but it remains invisible in the data. Individuals describe 'finally being calm' or 'getting my life together'.
interior_life.framing: Treatment and character. Quieter appetite is read as recovery, discipline or professional maturity. Among the affluent it is part of the uniform: composed, sober, lean.
interior_life.effect_on_work: HR and EAP vendors now route employees with heavy-drinking flags toward semaglutide under AUD parity coverage and report fewer absences. Managers in sales, hospitality and commission-based trades sometimes say their teams lack 'hunger', in the metaphorical sense, and no one writes down a cause. Corporate offsites are dry by default.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Bars, bowling leagues and late-night trivia lose middle-aged regulars, especially in Rust Belt towns, and the losses are attributed to cost and sobriety. Comedians build sets around 'my wife's on the pill, I'm on the waitlist'. Music writers note a continuing taste for loud, intense, high-sensation live formats among users. Some novelists and musicians credit the drug with sobriety; a few say they write less, and nobody follows up.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples therapists report more 'contented but flat' couples and more mismatched desire where one partner has coverage and the other does not. Sex-therapy podcasts discuss it openly. There is no clinical literature.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or participation. The 'sedated workforce' line is now used mostly by populist-right commentators against employers and pharma, and occasionally by labour organisers, which keeps the question politically coded and unstudied.

state.regulatory_posture: Restrictive at the edges, permissive at the core. The FDA approved oral amycretin and the AUD indication on schedule. In Jan 2030 it also finalised a rule ending the 'adequate provision' route for incretin obesity ads, which effectively ended TV and streaming spots for weight-management indications, and with the FTC it issued enforcement letters to telehealth firms paying influencers. Eleven states (incl. Florida, Texas, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Louisiana, Ohio, Utah) passed minor-prescribing restrictions in 2029–30. Ages 12–17 need an in-person paediatric-specialist visit, parental consent and a documented 6-month lifestyle programme before a prescription; under-12 use is banned in 6 of the states. Four states require an in-person visit before any first telehealth prescription for obesity. Personal importation remains effectively unpoliced.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare Continuity Model and Medicaid at the frozen $245, TrumpRx cash prices frozen at 2028 levels, and AUD coverage under existing parity and Medicaid substance-use benefits. Public obesity coverage still requires proof of adherence and response.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Medicare obesity coverage and nine Medicaid waivers require ≥80% refill adherence and ≥5% loss at 6 months, with a 12-month lockout on lapse. About 1 in 4 large self-funded employers run BMI-contingent wellness surcharges waived by biometric proof or by connected-pen or pill-bottle-sensor adherence data synced to wellness vendors. The state minor-restriction laws add a parental-consent registry in Florida and Tennessee. The Texas ban on BMI surcharges in state-regulated plans stands, and ERISA plans remain exempt.
state.workforce_or_military: Army and Air Force accession waivers for recruits who met standards on a GLP-1 continue, with ≥6 months of off-drug stability required. The Navy adopted the same policy in 2029. TRICARE covers obesity use for active duty only under strict criteria, and covers AUD use for active duty and dependents.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US–India price gap (~$199–449 vs ~$15) still runs through personal importation. Oral-peptide API capacity is the strategic bottleneck, and Novo and Lilly win tariff relief in exchange for US plant commitments. Canadian generic semaglutide is still bought by border-state residents. Import alerts on Indian API shippers continue, with limited effect on finished-product mail.

events.event: Business Group on Health survey: employer weight-management coverage falls to 39% from 44%, as Walmart-scale self-funded employers and two of the three largest airlines limit GLP-1s to diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnea codes; the 2030 survey shows 36%.

Pew survey: 58% of Americans say they can 'usually tell' someone's income from their body, up from 41% in 2026, and 1 in 4 workers under 40 say an employer or recruiter has commented on their fitness.

CMS renews the Medicare GLP-1 Continuity Model for 2030–31 at an unchanged $245 a month after Novo and Lilly decline further cuts, citing oral-peptide API shortages; TrumpRx prices stay where they were set in 2027–28.

FDA finalises a rule effectively ending broadcast and streaming ads for incretin weight-loss indications, joining 11 states that in 2029–30 restricted prescribing to minors and banned it under age 12 in six of them.
FDA approves Novo Nordisk's oral amycretin, the first pill to match tirzepatide's roughly 21% weight loss; it launches in May at $449 a month cash, with pharmacy waitlists within weeks.

FDA approves semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in adults of any weight, months after addiction-medicine societies endorsed it; under parity rules, many plans that exclude the drug for obesity must now cover it for drinking.

open_tensions: Parity versus exclusion: plans that refuse obesity coverage must cover the same molecule for AUD, so prescribers code for alcohol and PBMs audit for it. The fight over what a diagnosis is for will land in courts and in the 2031 Medicare budget, where obesity-only spending (~$7.1B/yr) already runs well above CBO's baseline.

Body as class uniform: coverage, cash price and gym access now map onto visible physique. Weight-discrimination suits are multiplying under the Michigan and NYC statutes while large self-funded employers keep BMI surcharges under ERISA.
The pill that matches the pen is supply-limited at $449 just as US generic semaglutide approaches in 2031–32. Whoever controls oral-peptide API capacity sets the price of the next tier.

The longest-exposed cohorts are crossing five years with only a hyposmia signal and no measure of reward blunting or of repeated cycling, while the drug's newest indication makes reduced wanting the endpoint. The first adolescent cohort turns 18 into a world of state age laws and no long-term data.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; brand exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, with oral initial doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) at $149/month.
Wegovy's list price is still $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay for covered obesity use under the Continuity Model.
The FDA's Jan 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels stands; it has not been reinstated.

prose.headline: The Body Is the Paystub: one in four Americans is on the drug, and you can tell which tier they're in
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2030 about 62 million American adults, nearly one in four, take an incretin drug, and another 20 million have taken one and stopped. The growth did not come from insurers. Employers kept leaving: barely a third still pay for weight management, and those that do want a diabetes or heart code first. The growth came from the pill, and from cash.

In April the FDA approved Novo Nordisk's oral amycretin, the first tablet to match tirzepatide's roughly 21 percent weight loss. The needle had been the last soft barrier, and now it is gone. More than half of new starts are oral. Making an oral peptide takes enormous amounts of active ingredient, though, so the new pill launched at $449 a month with pharmacy waitlists. For the first time since the drugs became ordinary, prices did not fall. TrumpRx still sells semaglutide at $199 and the starter pills at $149, as it did in 2028. Medicare still pays $245. The manufacturers say they have found a floor, and the government did not push.

In August semaglutide was approved for alcohol use disorder in people of any weight. That made reduced wanting a formal endpoint. It also opened a strange door: plans that exclude the drug for obesity often must cover it for drinking under mental-health parity rules. Some doctors now write the alcohol code, and pharmacy benefit managers have started auditing them. Employee-assistance programmes route heavy drinkers toward the pill and report fewer sick days.

The result is a country where body shape works as a pay slip. Professionals with coverage or cash, plus a trainer, wear a lean, muscled build that recruiters in Columbus and Charlotte admit, off the record, counts as executive presence. Menswear has re-cut its suits around shoulders and thighs. Cash users without a gym are thin and soft. Gray-market users, nine million of them, take Indian generics shipped through a personal-importation route nobody polices, at $60 to $120. Hourly workers at big self-funded employers pay $50 to $100 a month in BMI surcharges, waived if a connected pen or pill-bottle sensor reports adherence. A Pew survey found most Americans think they can tell someone's income from their body. Weight-discrimination suits are multiplying in Michigan and New York City.

The state has tightened at the edges and left the core alone. In January the FDA effectively ended television advertising for the weight indications, and the FTC went after telehealth influencers. Eleven states, Ohio, Florida and Texas among them, now require teenagers to see a paediatric specialist in person, bring parental consent and finish six months of a lifestyle programme before a prescription; six ban use under twelve. Child use has barely risen. The adults in those children's houses keep starting.

No new safety signal came. Europe closed its review of the smell-loss finding with a note to keep watching, and nobody has replicated or refuted it. Nobody measures what the drugs do to pleasure. The alcohol trials counted drinks, not joy. Users describe feeling calm, sober and finally grown up, and their employers agree.

Snack volumes are down several points from 2026 and spirits more, and distillers have written down American brands. Taverns in Rust Belt towns close one at a time, and the private-label snack plants in Indiana go with them. Strength gyms grow, and plus-size chains keep closing. The counter-movement has split along the same class line as everything else: fat-liberation organisers fight about coverage, 'Made Whole' congregations hold full-plate Sundays, and wellness influencers sell natural alternatives to people who could afford the drug anyway. Nothing has broken. You can see from across a parking lot who has which kind of insurance.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renee Kowalski, 52, clocks in at the distribution centre outside Columbus at 5:40. In the break room she swallows a white tablet, generic oral semaglutide from a pharmacy in Hyderabad, $72 a month through an app. The blister pack's label is in English and Hindi. She keeps it in her purse, not the cabinet.

At 9 the wellness kiosk asks her to step on the scale. She is still above 30. The $75 surcharge stays on her paycheck because the pills don't sync to anything. The company stopped covering hers in 2029.

The new regional manager walks the floor at lunch, forearms like a rower's. Someone says he's on the new pill, the $449 one with the waitlist. Nobody says it meanly.

Her husband Mike's prescription came through in September. His doctor wrote alcohol use disorder, which is true, and the plan paid. He's quit the Thursday league at Sully's, which is closing anyway. He sleeps well. He says he feels fine, and she believes him.

After her shift, her daughter Kayla, fifteen, is waiting in the car with the clinic paperwork. Ohio law: paediatric specialist, in person, both parents sign, six months of the programme first. The children's hospital's first opening is in June.

"Mom, girls at school just get it from their aunts."

"Not in this house."

Dinner is chicken thighs and green beans. Renee eats half. Mike eats half. Kayla eats everything and then a bowl of cereal, and Renee watches her do it. She doesn't know if what she feels is envy.
